extracted.intended_audience: institutional investors, BlackRock clients, company boards, and stewardship/voting teams
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluation criteria BlackRock Investment Stewardship (BIS) uses to engage with companies and make voting decisions on behalf of index equity clients, focusing on long-term financial materiality. Includes engagement priorities, board assessment criteria, contested election considerations, and voting rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing perceived and potential conflicts of interest in proxy voting
rubrics_metrics.description: We meet with the independent third-party voting service provider once a year to discuss any vote recommendations that seemed inconsistent with BIS’ regional voting guidelines and to explain any changes to these guidelines planned for the following year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain an Oversight Committee and annual engagement with the third‑party provider to review inconsistent recommendations and upcoming guideline changes. Evaluate the third‑party provider’s performance as part of BIS’ annual review and vendor due diligence (example: Glass Lewis retained in 2025 and 2026; performance to be evaluated end of 2026). These measures are intended to appropriately manage perceived and potential conflicts while ensuring exercise of clients’ voting rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmark Policies: financial materiality-based approach
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS Benchmark Policies take a financial materiality-based approach and are focused solely on advancing clients’ long-term financial interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the Benchmark Policies when engaging and voting, focusing on issues that are financially material to clients’ long‑term value. Note which clients have asked BIS to apply the Benchmark Policies (clients representing approximately three quarters of public equity AUM).

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement Priorities (framework for assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS frames engagement and voting through five Engagement Priorities used to assess company‑specific issues that may be financially material over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The five priorities (used as the analytical lens for case studies and engagements) are: Strategy, purpose, and financial resilience; Board quality and effectiveness; Incentives aligned with financial value creation; Climate and natural capital; Company impacts on people. Engagements often cover multiple topics; classify engagements by primary topic for statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engaging to build understanding of material risks and inform voting
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging with companies to build our understanding of material risks and opportunities and inform our voting decisions on behalf of our clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold targeted engagements (frequency and scope vary) to gather disclosures and context that inform voting. Track engagements by region, number of companies engaged, repeat engagements, and markets engaged. Use engagement outcomes to inform voting decisions and to deepen understanding of company business models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise voting rights to protect and enhance long-term financial value
rubrics_metrics.description: We exercise, on our clients’ behalf, the voting rights that help protect and enhance the long-term financial value of their assets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vote in a manner aligned with advancing clients’ long-term financial interests. Do not engage with portfolio companies for the purpose, or with the effect, of changing or influencing control of any company (comply with regulatory guidance such as SEC staff updates on Schedule 13G).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal taxonomy and evaluation by proposal type
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify and evaluate proposals by type (e.g., director elections and board-related proposals; executive compensation proposals; shareholder proposals) when making voting decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a clear taxonomy for proposals (BlackRock’s taxonomy used in reporting). Track proportions and apply evaluation criteria appropriate to each category (e.g., director election criteria differ from executive compensation or shareholder proposal review). Refer to appendix for full detail of proposal taxonomy when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary reasons for not supporting management on director elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Four key governance-related reasons BIS did not support management recommendations: director independence, executive compensation not aligned with shareholder interests, board composition, and director overcommitment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider these four issues as primary red flags when assessing support for management recommendations globally. Director independence was the primary driver of votes against management in 2025, especially in certain regions (e.g., APAC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons for not supporting climate and people shareholder proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Common reasons BIS did not support climate and natural capital, and company impacts on people shareholder proposals include: lacking economic merit; too prescriptive; company has process in place to address business risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess shareholder proposals on whether they present economic merit, whether they are overly prescriptive relative to company discretion, and whether the company already has adequate processes to address the stated business risk. A proposal may be unsupported for more than one reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to contested director elections and shareholder activism
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing contested director elections, BIS evaluates each activist situation individually and votes for the outcome most aligned with clients’ long-term financial interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage with both the company and the dissident. Consider: qualifications and past performance of candidates (management and dissident); the concerns identified by the dissident to justify board changes; viability of both plans to address valid concerns; ownership stake and holding period of the dissident; likelihood the dissident’s strategy will improve business and financial performance; whether dissident nominees would enhance the board’s ability to oversee and advise management. Prefer supporting management where the board can adequately address legitimate concerns and commit publicly to steps to do so, as this is often less disruptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board effectiveness — group-level criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong board is composed of appropriately qualified, engaged directors with professional characteristics relevant to the company’s business and enhances the board’s ability to add long-term financial value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess board effectiveness by evaluating relevance of individual directors’ qualifications/skillsets; directors’ capacity and time commitments; independence and independent leadership; board oversight of management strategy and risk; succession planning for key roles; and the board’s nomination and evaluation processes. Look for formal and transparent processes that reflect the company’s long-term strategy and business model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director independence standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Director independence — from management, significant shareholders, or other related parties — is a central tenet of sound corporate governance. BIS generally considers it good practice for independent directors to make up a majority of the board, or in the case of controlled companies, at least one-third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate independence relative to management and significant shareholders. Take into account local market codes and listing rules (e.g., Hong Kong requires at least three INEDs and INEDs to be at least one-third of the board; tenure limits apply). For long-serving directors (e.g., nine or more years), expect disclosure explaining the independent classification; absent such disclosure, BIS may not consider them independent and may not support re-election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director tenure disclosure and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a director has long tenure (e.g., nine or more years under Hong Kong rules), companies should disclose information explaining continued independent classification; BIS may not consider long-tenured directors independent without sufficient disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether Nomination/Governance Committee disclosures adequately explain how long-serving directors remain independent in judgment. If board composition falls below best‑practice thresholds (e.g., less than one‑third independent), this can trigger votes against re-election of long-tenured INEDs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board composition assessment factors
rubrics_metrics.description: In assessing board composition, BIS considers a company’s board size, business model, strategy, market capitalization, ownership structure, and the market in which the company operates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies should explain how board composition supports governance practices and provide sufficient information on individual director candidates so shareholders can assess capabilities, suitability, and fit within overall board composition. Tailor composition expectations to company context (sector, market norms, ownership structures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Director capacity and overcommitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Directors’ capacity and other time commitments are material factors when assessing board effectiveness and may be a reason to not support management recommendations (director overcommitment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate directors’ external commitments and whether they have sufficient time to fulfill duties; overcommitment is a recurring governance concern and may justify voting against re-election where it undermines effective oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement on CEO succession planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Succession planning — especially CEO succession planning — is a key board responsibility; BIS seeks to understand how boards approach both long-term transitions and emergency scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During engagements, discuss respective roles of the board and incumbent CEO, identification/development of internal successors versus external talent, and how companies support continuity and stability during leadership transitions. Use succession planning quality as part of board effectiveness assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of engagement outcomes in voting decisions (case study structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Case studies are presented with Background and Outcome sections: background gives company and proposal context and engagement description; outcome explains the voting decision and how engagement informed it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use engagements to obtain context and disclosure that inform whether to support management recommendations. Case studies illustrate applying a long-term, financially material lens; stewardship is not used to prescribe company actions or substitute for management strategy decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory/regulatory compliance in engagement and voting
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS complies with regulatory requirements (example: SEC guidance on Schedule 13G) and does not engage to alter beneficial ownership reporting eligibility or to influence control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure engagement activity does not conflict with securities law/regulator guidance. Disclose when regulatory considerations shape engagement approach (e.g., refrain from engagement that would change or influence control).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendor due diligence for third‑party voting providers
rubrics_metrics.description: Third‑party voting service providers (e.g., Glass Lewis) are subject to annual performance evaluation as part of BIS’ annual review and BlackRock’s vendor due diligence process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain independent providers, meet annually to discuss inconsistent recommendations relative to BIS regional guidelines, and include provider performance evaluation in vendor due diligence cycles.
